ety.text: From Middle English sitten, from Old English sittan, from Proto-West Germanic *sittjan, from Proto-Germanic *sitjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“sit”). Cognates Cognate with West Frisian sitte, Low German sitten, Dutch zitten, German sitzen, Swedish sitta, Norwegian Bokmål sitte, Norwegian Nynorsk sitja, Danish sidde, Faroese sita, Icelandic sitja; and with Irish suigh, Latin sedeo, Russian сиде́ть (sidétʹ).

senses.d: To be in a position in which the upper body is upright and supported by the buttocks.
ex: After a long day of walking, it was good just to sit and relax.
You're finishing the chowder if you sit there (motionless) all evening!

senses.d: To move oneself into such a position.
ex: I asked him to sit.

senses.d: To occupy a given position.
ex: The dishes are still sitting on the table!
The temple has sat atop that hill for centuries.

senses.d: To remain in a state of repose; to rest; to abide; to rest in any position or condition.
ex: And Moses said to […] the children of Reuben, Shall your brothren go to war, and shall ye sit here?
Like a demigod here sit I in the sky.

senses.d: To be a member of a deliberative body.
ex: I currently sit on a standards committee.

senses.d: Of a legislative or, especially, a judicial body such as a court, to be in session.
ex: In what city is the circuit court sitting for this session?

senses.d: To lie, rest, or bear; to press or weigh.
ex: The calamity sits heavy on us.

senses.d: To be adjusted; to fit.
ex: Your new coat sits well.
This new and gorgeous garment, majesty, / Sits not so easy on me as you think.

senses.d: To be accepted or acceptable; to work.
ex: How will this new contract sit with the workers?
I don’t think it will sit well.

senses.d: To cause to be seated or in a sitting posture; to furnish a seat to.
ex: Sit him in front of the TV and he might watch for hours.

senses.d: An act of sitting.
Subsidence of the roof of a coal mine.
An event, usually lasting one full day or more, where the primary goal is to sit in meditation.

ety.text: From Middle English situacioun, situacion, from Middle French situation, from Medieval Latin situatio (“position, situation”), from situare (“to locate, place”), from Latin situs (“a site”). By surface analysis, situate + -ion.

senses.d: The combination of circumstances at a given moment; a state of affairs.
ex: The United States is in an awkward situation with debt default looming.

senses.d: The way in which something is positioned vis-à-vis its surroundings.
ex: The Botanical Gardens are in a delightful situation on the river bank.

senses.d: The place in which something is situated; a location.
ex: [Hibíscus] speciòsus is the most splendid, and deserves a situation in every garden.

senses.d: Position or status with regard to conditions and circumstances.
A position of employment; a post.
ex: ‘Let me hear another sound from you,’ said Scrooge, ‘and you’ll keep your Christmas by losing your situation!
When he was nineteen, he suddenly left the 'Co-op' office, and got a situation in Nottingham.

senses.d: A difficult or unpleasant set of circumstances; a problem.
ex: Boss, we've got a situation here…

senses.d: An individual movie theater.
ex: This survey includes all key situations (including Paramount Gulf Theaters) as well as suburban runs and small-town situations.

senses.d: An outfit, garment, or look.
ex: She is working some sort of amazing burgundy chiffon situation with gold piping.

ety.text: From Middle English site, from Anglo-Norman site, from Latin situs (“position, place, site”), from sinere (“to put, lay, set down, usually let, suffer, permit”). Doublet of sitio and situs.

senses.d: The place where anything is fixed; situation; local position
ex: the site of a city or of a house
At the site of its termination in the bladder there was a diverticulum a few centimeters long.

senses.d: A place fitted or chosen for any certain permanent use or occupation
ex: a site for a church
Having given you an Account of the Site, Form, and other Ornaments of a Garden: I shall proceed to what remains for the beautifying of it, which is Flowers.

senses.d: The posture or position of a thing.
ex: Maintain site setbacks as far as possible from roadways and other routes providing rapid public access.

senses.d: A computer installation, particularly one associated with an intranet or internet service or telecommunications.
ex: The site with the DS3 connection can communicate back to our main network at 45 Mb/s.

From Middle English sittinge, sittynge, variant of sittinde, sittende, sittande, from Old English sittende (“sitting”), from Proto-Germanic *sitjandz (“sitting”), present participle of Proto-Germanic *sitjaną (“to sit”), equivalent to sit + -ing. Cognate with West Frisian sittend (“sitting”), Dutch zittend (“sitting”), German sitzend (“sitting”), Swedish sittande (“sitting”), Icelandic sitjandi (“sitting”).

senses.d: A period during which one is seated for a specific purpose.
ex: Due to the sheer volume of guests, we had to have two sittings for the meal.
The Queen had three sittings for her portrait.

senses.d: A seance or other session with a medium or fortuneteller.
A special seat allotted to a seat-holder, at church, etc.
The part of the year in which judicial business is transacted.
A legislative session (in the sense of meeting, and not period).
The incubation of eggs by a bird.
A clutch of eggs laid by a brooding bird.
ex: we have thirty-four chicks from eight sittings of eggs

senses.d: An uninterrupted application to anything for a time; the period during which one continues at anything.
ex: I read it in two sittings.

senses.d: Executed from a sitting position.
Occupying a specific official or legal position; incumbent.
ex: It is an iron rule of French politics that sitting presidents are detested.

senses.d: Of a bird, incubating eggs.

senses.d: Located in a specific place.
